questions.learningObjective: Explain the offer made to the garrison before the fort fell
questions.stem: One member of the Harwood Street group asks what the government actually offered the garrison before the fort surrendered. Explain the offer and why it mattered.

answer.exemplar: The offer was evacuation, but only after a relief ship arrived, so that the withdrawal would look like a planned evacuation rather than a surrender to force. It mattered because the Union was not conceding the fort's loss: the government intended to resupply the garrison first, and only to empty it once the fleet had shown it would not be taken by storm.

questions.explanation: The Union offered resupply first and evacuation later, so the garrison would not be handed over under threat. The Confederates refused that sequencing and demanded the fort's immediate surrender.
questions.hint: Ask what the relief ship was meant to signal.

questions.topic: Why a blockade must be effective
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a blockade had to be enforced and not merely declared

stimulus.body: A note circulated among the drafting states explained that a blockade is not made binding on neutral nations by announcement alone, but by actual force applied to the commerce of the blockaded state. Neutral powers were required by the note to respect any blockade on announcement

options.text: The note argued that blockades could only be justified in time of declared war

options.text: The note said merchant ships were exempt from any search or seizure
options.misconception: Believes neutral ships were untouchable

questions.explanation: The note treats a blockade as effective only when it is actually enforced against commerce. That is why the Union had to seize ships and hold the ports rather than merely publish a declaration of closure.

answer.exemplar: The declarations of secession charged the northern states with a deliberate breach of the compact: refusal to enforce the fugitive slave law, the admission of California as a free state under popular sovereignty, and the whole course of the Kansas legislature fight. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a blockade must be effective
questions.learningObjective: Explain the legal and practical reason a blockade had to be enforced
questions.stem: A revision of the blockade lists four reasons. Explain why a blockade had to be enforced rather than merely proclaimed.

answer.exemplar: International usage held that a blockade binds neutral shipping only where it is actually maintained, so a declaration on paper carried no force against a power with merchant ships. Enforcement meant sending warships to seize contraband carriers and hold the ports, which is why the Union's early failures to catch neutral vessels were treated as a serious diplomatic problem rather than a minor inconvenience.

questions.explanation: Neutral powers could ignore a blockade that was not enforced, so a proclamation alone closed nothing. The Union therefore had to seize ships and hold ports, which is what made the early leaks so damaging.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A plan of blockade and rivers
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the river and the sea aims of the plan worked together
questions.stem: The Oakdale circle examines the blockade declaration and the plan behind it. Explain how the two aims of the river and the sea worked together.

answer.exemplar: The river and the sea attacked the same weakness from different ends: the Mississippi carried the Confederacy's western produce to foreign buyers, and the southern ports carried its cotton to the same buyers. Taking the river without closing the ports would have driven traffic to the sea, and closing the ports without the river would have left a route inland, so the plan treated both as one problem.

questions.explanation: Taking the river closed an inland route to foreign trade, and the blockade closed the sea route. Together they removed the Confederacy's ability to sell its produce abroad and buy goods in return.
questions.hint: Ask where the Confederacy's exports actually left.

questions.topic: The war measure and foreign opinion
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the seizure of envoys changed opinion in Britain
questions.stem: Members of the Cedar Street group examine the seizure of two envoys from a mail steamer. Explain why the episode changed opinion in Britain.

answer.exemplar: The boarding was justified as a right of visit to a ship carrying dispatches, but taking two men off a British vessel was read in Britain as an act of war against the government itself, whatever the legal argument. questions.explanation: Taking envoys from a British ship made the action look like an insult to the flag, and the disavowal only half repaired it. British opinion hardened against the Confederacy and closer to the United States.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The conditions offered before the fort surrendered
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the sequence of the demands mattered
questions.stem: The Sable Hollow circle revises the disagreement over the fort's terms. Explain why the sequence of demands mattered as much as the demands themselves.

answer.exemplar: A bombardment timed to a demand is a demonstration rather than a duel, and the government understood the difference: the ship was ordered first so that the garrison would hold the fort and only withdraw when further resistance was pointless. The Confederates reversed the sequence by pressing for surrender before the ship arrived, and the result was that the fort fell by gunfire in a single night rather than by any surrender negotiated between two commands.

questions.explanation: The Union's plan had the fort held and then withdrawn, while the Confederates demanded its surrender before the resupply arrived. The reversed sequence produced gunfire rather than a negotiated handover.
questions.hint: Ask which side changed the order of events.

questions.topic: Why a blockade must be effective
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a foreign assessment of the blockade's effectiveness

stimulus.body: The memorandum advises that a blockade which is not maintained is a blockade in name only, and that nations with merchant shipping will not submit their trade to a mere proclamation; it adds that the government of the United States has at present no force afloat sufficient to enforce the restriction upon the trade of the Gulf and the lower coast.

questions.stem: The Vantage group revises the foreign assessment quoted above. Which conclusion is best supported?

The memorandum credited the United States with an adequate force at sea

options.text: The memorandum recommended immediate recognition of the Confederate States

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The proclamation as a war measure
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the legal structure of the freeing order

stimulus.body: All persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free; and the Executive Government of the United States, including the military and naval authority thereof, will recognise and maintain the freedom of such persons, and will do no act or acts to repress such persons, or any of them, in any efforts they may make for their actual freedom.

questions.stem: Members of the Pecker Street circle reconsiders the legal shape of the order. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: The order frees people by presidential action and depends on the army to hold the ground
The order is a statute of Congress and takes effect without any military action
options.misconception: Believes Congress passed the order

options.text: The order applies to every slave in the country on the date of signing
options.misconception: Believes the order was universal

options.text: The order asks the courts to declare slavery void in the states in rebellion
options.misconception: Believes the courts were asked to act

questions.explanation: The order speaks of the executive and military authority maintaining freedom and is confined to places in rebellion, so it is a war act, not a statute or a ruling. Its reach is exactly as far as the army can go.
questions.hint: Ask who the document names as the authority.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The constitutional question in secession
questions.learningObjective: Explain why argument alone could not settle the question of separation
questions.stem: The Harwood Street circle revises why the question of separation could not be settled by argument alone. Explain the difficulty the group identified.

answer.exemplar: Each side held a view of the Constitution that the other could not accept: one read the instrument as a compact among states, the other as an enduring national instrument, and each view was defended by a plausible reading of the same words. The dispute could not be settled by a vote of either section, because each side's answer carried the votes of its own states, and it was therefore a question that had to be settled by force if it was to be settled at all.

questions.explanation: Both positions had serious arguments and each commanded its own section's votes, so argument alone could not decide the matter. The Constitution offered no agreed procedure for such a disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask why a vote could not settle the dispute.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A plan of blockade and rivers
questions.learningObjective: Identify the measures the plan asked for

stimulus.body: The paper sets out that the enemy's coast shall be closed to all trade by a strict blockade, that the great river shall be taken and held from the Gulf to its sources, that the line of the Red River shall be closed so that the western reach of the rebellion shall be cut off, and that a force shall then move forward by the coast. It remarks that these measures are to be pursued with patience, since the strength of the enemy is in his resources and not in his numbers.

questions.stem: A source sheet on the plan prompts the question of what the document asked for. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: A blockade, command of the river, closure of the western route, then a coastal advance
A direct march on the capital, to be made before any measure of the sea
options.misconception: Believes the capital came first

options.text: The immediate enlistment of large numbers of regular troops for a land campaign
options.misconception: Believes the plan was a mass mobilisation

options.text: A negotiated settlement, to be reached by offering concessions to the southern states
options.misconception: Believes the plan was diplomatic

questions.explanation: The document names the blockade, the river, the Red River and a later coastal move, in that order, and it asks for patience. Its method is to exhaust the enemy's resources before committing to a direct assault.
questions.hint: Ask what the paper says the enemy's strength lay in.
